senses.gloss:
yuddha
(‘war’)
------------------------------------------
Though अहिṁसा or non-violence has been declared as paramadharma (highest virtue), the Hindu scriptures have not forgotten the need for हिṁसा (force, violence) while handling the criminals and the enemies of the society.
The Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 174.45) unequivocally declares that before the spiritual power of a ब्राह्मण, the military might of a क्षत्त्रिय pales into insignificance.
Normally a king is expected to rule over his own kingdom according to धर्म or righteousness and never interfere with the administration of other kings.
However, if other kings are bent upon invading his kingdom or create trouble, he is free to adopt all means at his disposal to thwart them, including युद्ध or war.
A king, while dealing with another king, especially if the latter is irascible and ambitious, is advised to adopt in the beginning the first three upāyas or means viz., sāma (reconciliation), दान (mutual rewards) and bheda (divide and rule policy). If none of these works, only then can he resort to दण्ड or war.
In any war, during the ancient days, both the combatants were expected to follow some standard ethical rules. The Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparva 1.27-32), the Rāmāyaṇa (Yuddhakāṇḍa 18.27, 28), the Manusmṛti (7.90-93), the Śukranīti (4.7.354-362) and other works deal with these rules. A few of these may be stated here: Fighting should be between equals, similarly equipped. One should not kill anyone fighting with another or who is running away from the battlefield or who pleads for mercy; so also one who has lost his horse or chariot or weapons or stops fighting. Treacherous means or poisoned weapons should never be used.
Though these rules are generally stated and accepted by most of the writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस्, कौटिल्य (300 B. C.) of the Arthaśāstra fame has his own, strong, views.
A powerful king with high ambitions naturally sets his eyes on the expansion of his kingdom by conquering other kings. Such a one is called vijigīṣu (‘one desirous of conquering’). कौटिल्य gives detailed instructions to such vijigīṣus.
The vijigīṣu king can recruit men from all the four varṇas for his armed forces, though the kṣattriyas, due to their inherent fighting spirit, form the core.
There should be a permanent, well-trained, standing army.
In addition, fighting forces should be raised during invasions or emergencies by paying higher wages or getting them from allies.
A well-planned army generally comprised four divisions—hence the name caturaṅgadala—viz., infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants. There had to be practice of the fighting arts everyday except on declared holidays.
This had to be ably supported by an armoury, stores containing ड़ोओद् articles and other essential supplies as also medical and paramedical staff.
Yāna or invasion had to be meticulously planned by the king with the assistance of his ministers and others. Friends had to be mobilised and enemies had to be neutralised. Espionage had to be strengthened. A reliable regent (called śūnyapāla) should be appointed to take care of the kingdom during the king’s absence.
Yuddha has been described as of three types: prakāśayuddha (open fight); kūṭayuddha (concealed fighting or tactical warfare); tūṣṇīṁyuddha (silent fight or using secret agents for enticing the enemies).
The existence of naval forces is indicated by the words such as nimna-yodhin (fighter in water).
Some of the other related topics dealt with in कौटिल्य’s work are: appointment of suitable officers in various grades; organisation of skandhavāsa or camps during the war; formation of the forces into several व्यूहस् like दण्ड-vyūha (staff-array), bhogavyūha (serpent-array), मण्डल vyūha (circular-array) and so on; placement of one-third or one-fourth of the mobilised troops to protect the kingdom; extra troops for guarding the rear.
It may be interesting to note that the Arthaśāstra mentions several types of weapons and implements of war as follows: sāṅgrāmika (weapons useful in the battle-field); daurgakarmika (weapons needed for defending the fort); parapurābhighātika (weapons needed for battering down an enemy’s fort).
The implements are: यन्त्र (machines); आयुध (weapons proper); आवरण (shields); upakaraṇa (other equipment).
A large number of machines are described, the principal purpose of which appears to be to throw huge stones at the enemy troops.
The section on the armoury also mentions aindrajālikakarma (magical rites) and aupaniṣadikakarma (secret practices).
There is another classification of weapons used in war. According to this, the weapons can be yantramukta (discharged from a contrivance like a bow or a sling), pāṇimukta (thrown with the hand, such as a stone or a discus), muktāmukta (which can be used directly or thrown like a spear), amukta (used by hand like a sword) and niyuddha (wrestling).
The epics and the पुराणस् are replete with the names of several astras like Āgneyāstra, Aindrāstra and ब्रह्मास्त्र. They are arrows discharged after infilling them with power through appropriate mantras. This science called astravidyā had to be properly learnt from a competent teacher.
When a king conquers another kingdom he is advised to install the son or a suitable relative of the defeated king if he has been killed. People of the conquered territory should be well taken care of, without disturbing their religion, culture and way of life. This is the best way to win them over.
Unethical practices including harassing the people of the enemy’s country was strictly forbidden.
See also RĀJYĀṄGAS.

Yuddhakāṇḍa
------------------------------------------
This is the sixth book of the famous epic Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि.
See RĀMĀYAṆA for details.
